title: 203/EXEC means systemd never even got the program running
explanation: `systemctl status apiserver` reporting `status=203/EXEC` is a specific pre-flight failure code from systemd itself, not an app crash — it means the fork happened but the `exec()` syscall on the `ExecStart=` program failed. That distinction matters: there's no application log to chase here, because the application's own code never ran.

title: See what path the unit is actually trying to run
explanation: `systemctl cat apiserver` shows the effective `ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/apiserver`. `203/EXEC` almost always reduces to one of three things: the path doesn't exist, it exists but isn't executable, or it's a script missing its shebang/interpreter — checking `ls -l /usr/local/sbin/apiserver` next narrows it down immediately.

title: Find where the binary really ended up
explanation: The path in the unit doesn't exist, but the package clearly installed the binary somewhere — `command -v apiserver` or a quick `ls -l /usr/local/bin/` locates it. The unit file is just stale relative to where the package now puts things after the move.

title: Edit the unit, then reload before restarting
explanation: Fixing `ExecStart=` to point at the real path only changes the file on disk. systemd caches parsed unit definitions in memory, so `systemctl daemon-reload` is required before `systemctl restart apiserver` will actually pick up the new path — skipping it means you'd be restarting the exact same broken definition you just edited.

title: Confirm against the same check that first surfaced the problem
explanation: `systemctl is-active apiserver` reporting `active` confirms the fix took, using the same status lens the incident started with — rather than assuming the edit worked just because `daemon-reload` and `restart` both returned without error.
